title: Queen against pawn: the draws
summary: The two pawns that escape the staircase of checks: stalemate in the corner, the zone where the king still wins, and the defender's resources.
part.rook.title: Rook pawn: the corner stalemates
part.rook.summary: Why the staircase of checks fails when the pawn is on the a-file.
part.block.title: The queen in front of the pawn
part.block.summary: If the black king leaves the promotion square, the queen stops on it and wins.
part.rookZone.title: Rook pawn: a close king wins
part.rookZone.summary: With the king in the zone, the queen lets the pawn promote and mates.
part.bishop.title: Bishop pawn: Petrosian against Fischer

part.bishopZone.title: Bishop pawn: Lolli and the long side

part.leko.summary: Promote to force the trade and bring the king to the corner; the three rules and the practical challenge.
step.t_rook: Rook pawn on a2, the black king beside it, our king far away. In the previous lesson, the staircase of checks put the black king in front of the pawn and our king gained a step. Does the staircase work here? What changes with the pawn on the a-file?
step.t_rook.hint1: Try the staircase and see where the black king goes on the last check.
step.t_rook.hint2: On the last check, find the square the black king can still go to, and count his squares there.
step.rookWhy: This is the end of the attempt. The black king is on a1, in front of the pawn, just as we wanted. But now Black has no move at all: the king cannot leave and the pawn cannot advance. If the queen stays where it is, it is stalemate. With a central pawn the king had the other side of the pawn to step out to. On the a-file there is no other side. So the queen has to release the pressure, the black king goes back to b2 and everything starts again.
step.d_rook: See the whole staircase, and where it gets stuck. White's moves are the ones from the previous lesson.
step.d_rook.m1: 1.Qd4+. The diagonal check takes b2 from the king and brings the queen close to the pawn.
step.d_rook.m2: 1...Kb1! The only move. On b1 the king guards a1; on the other squares he lets go of a1, and the queen wins. You will see how in the next part.
step.d_rook.m3: 2.Qb4+. The queen takes b2 and b3 from the king and wants to push him to a1, the square in front of the pawn.
step.d_rook.m4: 2...Kc2. The king steps out of check, but stays one step from b1 and b2.
step.d_rook.m5: 3.Qa3. No check: the queen attacks the pawn and takes b2 from the king.
step.d_rook.m6: 3...Kb1. The king defends the pawn again and guards a1 once more.
step.d_rook.m7: 4.Qb3+. Now the black king seems forced to go in front of the pawn.
step.d_rook.m8: 4...Ka1! He goes, and it is stalemate unless the queen moves away. White has gained no time at all: a draw.
step.rookHold: Now you defend, in an analysis by Paul Keres. After 1.Qg2+ Kb1 2.Qf1+ Kb2 3.Qb5+, the queen checks along the b-file, and the white king is on a8. Always bring the king close to the pawn, all the way to the corner.
step.rookHold.hint: Stay next to the pawn. If the queen attacks it without check, go back to the square that defends it.
step.rookHold.done: 3...Kc2, 4...Kb2, 5...Kc2, 6...Kb1 and 7...Ka1. The king never left the area around a1, and the queen cannot drive him out without stalemating. Keres gives this line in his book on practical endings.
step.t_block: The staircase from the first part. After 1.Qd4+, Black did not play 1...Kb1, the only move, but 1...Kc1?, which looks the same. What changed? Do the usual checks still work, or is there something better?
step.t_block.hint1: Look at the square the pawn has to pass through.
step.t_block.hint2: Can the black king still reach that square? And what if the queen gets there first?
step.blockWhy: This is the simplest rule of this ending. If the queen can stop on the square in front of the pawn without being captured, it wins: from there it guards b1 and b2, the black king cannot come closer and the pawn cannot advance. With 1...Kb1 the king guarded a1. With 1...Kc1? it no longer does. Before giving check, always look at the promotion square.
step.d_block: Watch the queen stop in front of the pawn.
step.d_block.m1: 2.Qa1+! The queen stops on the square in front of the pawn, and with check too. The squares b1 and b2 are now guarded.
step.d_block.m2: 2...Kd2. The black king can no longer defend a2: the pawn is on its own.
step.d_block.m3: 3.Qxa2+. The pawn falls, and what is left is queen against king, a mate you already know.
step.blockMove: Now on the other side of the board: pawn on h2, the black king on f1 and our king far away on b8. Find the winning move.
step.blockMove.hint: The staircase checks get nowhere. Look at the square the pawn has to pass through: can the queen get there before the black king?
step.blockMove.done: 1.Qh1+! The queen reached the square in front of the pawn before the black king did: the pawn cannot move any more, and 2.Qxh2+ captures it.
step.t_rookZone: Same pawn on a2, but now our king is on d5. Is he close enough? How do we win, if the staircase does not work?
step.t_rookZone.hint1: You do not need to stop the pawn from promoting. Ask what happens afterwards.
step.t_rookZone.hint2: With the white king on b3, the queen has two mating squares near the corner.
step.rookZoneWhy: The marked squares are the zone: with the white king on any of them, and the queen giving check, White wins. From there the king reaches b3 in at most two moves, or d3 and d2 in one. The idea is new: instead of holding the pawn back, we let it promote. The new queen is stuck in the corner, and our king and queen mate before it can do anything.
step.d_rookZone: Watch the move that looks like a mistake: the white king lets the pawn promote.
step.d_rookZone.m1: 1.Kc4! The king heads for b3 and lets the pawn promote.
step.d_rookZone.m2: 1...a1=Q. Black has a queen again, but it is in the corner, behind its own king.
step.d_rookZone.m3: 2.Qd2+. The check sends the black king back to the first rank, and his queen stays shut in the corner.
step.d_rookZone.m4: 2...Kb1. The king goes back to b1; after 2...Ka3 the mate would come even sooner.
step.d_rookZone.m5: 3.Kb3! The king takes a2, b2 and c2 from the black king. The threat is 4.Qd1 and 4.Qc2, both mate, and the black queen, stuck behind its own king, can only delay it.
step.rookZoneMove: Your turn, in a training position by TonyRo. The white king is on a5, two moves from b3. Use checks to keep the black king near the corner and bring your king to b3, even if the pawn promotes.
step.rookZoneMove.hint: Once the queen guards the first rank and the black king is on b2, your king can walk.
step.rookZoneMove.done: 1.Qb3+, 2.Qd1+, 3.Kb4!, 4.Qd2+ and 5.Kb3. It is the same picture as in the demonstration: the king on b3 and the queen ready to mate on d1 or c2.
step.t_bishop: Petrosian against Fischer, Portorož Interzonal, 1958. White has just played 67.f7, and the pawn is about to promote. You have Black, like Fischer. Can Black save the game? With what plan?
step.t_bishop.hint1: The rook cannot stop both white pawns. What is left if it leaves the board?
step.t_bishop.hint2: Imagine a white queen against your c-pawn already on the seventh, with your king beside it. Where would the white king be?
step.pfWhy: The two players, both future world champions, agreed a draw here. Fischer gives the line in the book of his best games: the rook gives itself up for the g-pawn, the black king goes near the a1 corner and the c-pawn reaches the seventh. It becomes queen against bishop pawn, with the white king far away on g6.
step.d_fischer: The line Fischer gives in the book.
step.d_fischer.m1: 67...Rxg6+! The rook gives itself up for the g-pawn, with check: only one white pawn is left.
step.d_fischer.m2: 68.Kxg6. The white king captures, but he stands on g6, far from the queenside.
step.d_fischer.m3: 68...Kb1. The king goes to the side of the a1 corner, right next to the pawn's path.
step.d_fischer.m4: 69.f8=Q. White has a queen, but the white king is far away.
step.d_fischer.m5: 69...c2. Bishop pawn on the seventh, the king beside it and the white king far away: a draw.
step.bishopWhy: This is the bishop pawn's trick. The black king hides on a1, in the corner next to the pawn. If White plays 1.Qxc2, the king has no square at all: a2, b1 and b2 are guarded, and it is stalemate. If the queen does not capture, the pawn promotes. Even with the white king on e4, much closer than Petrosian's, White does not win: the corner is not in front of the pawn but beside it, and the stalemate is the same.
step.fischerHold: Now you defend, like Fischer. From the book position, White tries 70.Qb4+. Keep the king next to the pawn and use the a1 corner when the queen closes in.
step.fischerHold.hint: The a1 corner is your hiding place: with the king there, capturing the pawn is stalemate.
step.fischerHold.done: 70...Ka2, 71...Kb1 and 72...Ka1. Now 73.Qxc2 is stalemate, and any other queen move lets the king out. White has made no progress: it is the draw both players saw over the board.
step.t_lolli: A position from 1763. The black king is on d1, on the long side of the pawn, far from the a1 corner. Our king is on g4. How do we stop the black king from reaching the corner, and how do we bring our king over?
step.t_lolli.hint1: First shut the door: the black king wants to go to b1 or b2.
step.t_lolli.hint2: Then the white king walks. If the pawn promotes when the white king is close, there is a mate with the queen on e2.
step.bishopZoneWhy: Against the bishop pawn the zone is smaller. With the black king on b2, White wins if his king reaches b3 or d2 in a single move: those are the marked squares, a4, b4, c4, d3, e3, d2, e2 and e1. From here, on e4, he is one step from the zone. That is why the side the black king is on matters so much. The short side is the side of the a1 corner; the long side is the side of the centre. The defender runs to the short side. The attacker keeps him on the long side, preferably with a quiet move, which does not give the black king a choice of squares.
step.d_lolli: Giambattista Lolli's study, from 1763. The black king is on the long side, and the queen does not let him cross.
step.d_lolli.m1: 1.Qb3! A quiet move: the queen guards b1 and c2 and shuts the way to the corner.
step.d_lolli.m2: 1...Kd2. The black king stays on the long side, because b1 and b2 are shut.
step.d_lolli.m3: 2.Qb2. The queen guards c1, b1 and a1 and attacks the pawn.
step.d_lolli.m4: 2...Kd1. The king leaves the second rank so that the pawn can promote.
step.d_lolli.m5: 3.Kf3! The king comes, and from f3 he protects e2: if the pawn promotes, the queen mates there.
step.d_lolli.m6: 3...c1=Q. The pawn promotes. The most stubborn defence was 3...Kd2, but the white king would arrive all the same.
step.d_lolli.m7: 4.Qe2#. The queen mates, protected by the king on f3: this is the long-side mate.
step.bishopZoneMove: Now you finish. The black king is on c1, in front of the pawn, and our king comes along the b-file.
step.bishopZoneMove.hint: The king goes to b3, where he helps with the mate. The queen holds the pawn on the way.
step.bishopZoneMove.done: 1.Kb4, 2.Qd2 and 3.Kb3. If the pawn promotes, 4.Qa2 is mate; if it becomes a knight with check, the king steps out of check and the mate comes all the same. This is the zone at work: the king reached b3.
step.t_extra: The stalemate picture from the first part, with one difference: Black has an extra pawn on h3. Capturing it looks natural. What does that pawn change, and how does White win?
step.t_extra.hint1: Count the moves the black king has now. And the h-pawn?
step.t_extra.hint2: Leave the h-pawn alive and look for a move without check that keeps the black king locked in.
step.extraWhy: Without the h-pawn, this would be the drawn position: with the black king on a1, every waiting move by the queen gave stalemate. 1.Qxh3? sends Black back to that draw, because the king gets b1 and b2 again. With the pawn alive, Black is forced to move it, and the king stays locked in the corner. Stalemate only exists when the defender has no move at all; a pawn that can still move takes that defence away.
step.d_extra.m1: 1.Qc2! A quiet move. The black king has no square, because b1 and b2 are guarded. Without the h-pawn, this would be stalemate.
step.d_extra.m2: 1...h2. Black's only move, and it does not help.
step.d_extra.m3: 2.Qc1#. Mate on the first rank: Black's own pawn on a2 takes the king's last square.
step.extraMove: Your turn. The staircase from the first part, now with an extra black pawn on g6. Drive the black king into the corner and finish.
step.extraMove.hint: Once the black king enters a1, do not capture anything: take his last squares and let the g-pawn move.
step.extraMove.done: 1.Qb3+ Ka1, 2.Qc2! and 3.Qc1#. The g-pawn forced Black to move, and the corner became a prison. If 1...Kc1, 2.Qxa2: the king left the corner, as in the second part.
step.t_knight: You have Black, with the pawn on f2. The white king has reached e3, the queen is on h2 and your king is on e1, next to the promotion square. The corner is far away and there is no stalemate in sight. How does Black save the game?
step.t_knight.hint1: Before promoting to a queen, see what the white queen does on d2.
step.t_knight.hint2: Look for a new piece that gives check and attacks something else at the same time.
step.knightWhy: 1...f1=Q? loses to 2.Qd2, mate. The right piece is the knight: from f1 it checks the king on e3 and attacks the queen on h2 at the same time. That is the fork. White moves the king out of check, and the knight captures the queen. King and knight against king cannot mate.
step.d_knight.m1: 1...f1=N+! Check, and the knight attacks the queen on h2.
step.d_knight.m2: 2.Kf3. The king steps out of check, but from no square can he protect the queen.
step.d_knight.m3: 2...Nxh2+. King and knight against king: nobody can mate. A draw.
step.knightMove: The same pawn on f2, with the white pieces on other squares: the king on g3 and the queen on d2. Your king is on g1. Find the drawing move.
step.knightMove.hint: Promoting to a queen loses: the white queen mates on h2. From f1, which squares can a new piece reach?
step.knightMove.done: 1...f1=N+! and 2...Nxd2+. From f1 the knight reaches g3 and d2 at the same time. When promoting to a queen loses and the corner is no help, look at the knight: the check gains the time to capture the queen.
step.t_leko: Van Wely against Leko, Tilburg, 1996. White has just played 57.g6: the pawn will promote on g8, and the rook on a5 attacks your a2-pawn and, behind it, the promotion square. You are Leko, with Black. What is the plan to draw?
step.t_leko.hint1: The white rook is tied to your a-pawn. How do you take it off the board?
step.t_leko.hint2: Think about where your king will be when the c-pawn reaches the seventh.
step.lekoWhy: Leko played 57...a1=Q. The new queen is protected by the king, and the rook has to capture it: 58.Rxa1 Kxa1. The king recaptures and is already in the corner, next to the square the c-pawn will pass through. Promoting on a square your king defends forces the attacker to trade, and the recapturing king already stands where it needs to be.
step.d_leko.m1: 57...a1=Q! The new queen is protected by the king on b2.
step.d_leko.m2: 58.Rxa1. White has to capture, or be a queen down.
step.d_leko.m3: 58...Kxa1. The king recaptures and is already in the corner.
step.d_leko.m4: 59.g7. The white pawn is one step from promoting. Now Black has only one move.
step.lekoMove: Your turn, like Leko. The white pawn promotes next move. Find the drawing move, and then the next one.
step.lekoMove.hint: Your pawn has to reach the seventh in time, with the king beside the corner.
step.lekoMove.done: 59...c3! and 60...c2, as Leko played. It is the bishop pawn on the seventh with the king on a1 and the white king on h7: here the players agreed a draw. 59...Kb2? lost: after 60.g8=Q c3, the pawn is still on the sixth and the queen wins.
step.recap: This is the final position of Van Wely against Leko. Three rules to take with you. One: a rook or bishop pawn on the seventh, with its king beside it and the white king far away, draws by stalemate; but if the black king leaves the promotion square, the queen stops in front and wins. Two: with the white king in the zone, let the pawn promote and mate; and if Black has an extra pawn, the stalemate disappears. Three: the defender takes the king to the corner, and when the corner is not enough, looks at the promotion: the protected piece that forces the trade, or the knight with check.
step.finish: Now the practical challenge: you have the bishop pawn, White has the queen and a distant king. Keep your king next to the pawn, on the corner side, and do not fall into the traps.
ex.e12: White to move. Bishop pawn on f2, the black king on g3, our king far away on h8. Checks get nowhere here. Win.
ex.e12.hint: Look at the square in front of the pawn. Is the black king guarding it?
ex.e12.solution: 1.Qf1! The queen stops in front of the pawn, on a square the black king cannot reach. Now the pawn cannot move, and our king walks over from h8 to take it. Checks such as 1.Qg6+ let the black king reach the corner, and then it was the usual draw. The rule: if the queen can stand in front of the pawn, it is over.
ex.e04: Black to move. The white queen is on e1, on the promotion rank. The white king is far away. Which is the only move that draws?
ex.e04.hint: If the king leaves the pawn, the queen will stand in front of it.
ex.e04.solution: 1...c1=Q! The new queen is protected by the king, and after 2.Qxc1+ Kxc1 only the kings are left. Any king move allowed 2.Qc1, the queen blockading the pawn, and the white king would come and take it.
ex.e13: Black to move. The black king is in the a1 corner, but the white king has already reached b3: stalemate no longer saves Black. Only one move draws.
ex.e13.hint: Promoting to a queen loses, and the king has nowhere to go. Look for a new piece that gives check.
ex.e13.solution: 1...c1=N+! The knight checks the king on b3 and attacks the queen on d3 at the same time. The white king has to move, and 2...Nxd3 leaves king and knight against king: a draw. 1...c1=Q? lost to 2.Qa6+ and mate, and 1...Kb1 to 2.Qxc2+. When the king and the queen stand on squares a new knight reaches together, look at the underpromotion.
ex.e10: White to move. Bishop pawn on f2, the black king on e2, not yet in the corner. Our king is on e5. This is a position by Snape. Win.
ex.e10.hint: Checks that keep the black king away from the h1 corner, so our king gains time.
ex.e10.solution: 1.Qc4+ (or 1.Qg4+, 1.Qa2+ or the quiet 1.Qg2) 1...Ke1, 2.Qe4+ Kf1 and 3.Kf4. The black king reaches the corner, but too late: after 3...Kg1 4.Qd4 Kh1, 5.Kg3! and, if the pawn promotes, 6.Qh8+ leads to mate. 5.Qxf2 at any moment with the king on h1 would be stalemate.
ex.e14: White to move. It looks like the bishop pawn draw: the black king on g1, our king on b5, much too far. But Black has an extra pawn on h7. Win.
ex.e14.hint: The h7 pawn can still move. What does that change when the black king goes to the h1 corner?
ex.e14.solution: 1.Qg4+ (or 1.Qg8+) 1...Kh2, 2.Qf3 Kg1, 3.Qg3+ (or 3.Qg4+, 3.Qe3) and, if 3...Kh1, 4.Qxf2. It is not stalemate: Black still has the h7 pawn to move, and the queen alone holds a rook pawn that has not even left home. The extra pawn takes the stalemate defence away from Black. Beware of 1.Qc1+?, which even loses: 1...f1=Q+ blocks with check and, after 2.Qxf1+ Kxf1, it is the h7 pawn that will queen, because our king is far away. The position is analysed by Müller and Lamprecht.
ex.e16: White to move. Rook pawn on a2, the black king on c3, our king far away on g5. The black king has not reached the corner yet. Find the way, one move at a time.
ex.e16.hint: Do not check. First take b2 away from the black king, then the long diagonal to the corner.
ex.e16.solution: 1.Qe2! takes b2 away from the black king. After 1...Kb3, 2.Qe5! watches the diagonal down to a1, and after 2...Kc2, 3.Qa1! The queen stands in front of the pawn, and the white king comes to collect it. Checks let the black king reach b2 and a1, and stalemate saved Black. Three quiet moves, and each one is the only win.
ex.e15: White to move. Bishop pawn on c2, the black king on e3, on the long side. Our king is far away on h6. Find the way, one move at a time.
ex.e15.hint: The black king wants to cross to the a1 corner side. Cut him off without checking, then put the queen in front of the pawn.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Qg2! cuts off the second rank: the black king cannot reach d2. After 1...Kd3, 2.Qg5! watches c1 and d2 from a distance, and after 2...Kc3, 3.Qc1! The queen is in front of the pawn and the white king comes to collect it. Checks pushed the black king to b2 and a1, the short side, and that was a draw. The quiet 2.Qg5 is Glenn Flear's idea: from a distance, the queen watches the squares the black king would use to reach the pawn.
key.rookDraw: Rook pawn about to queen and the white king far away: when the queen corners the black king, it runs out of moves and it is stalemate. A draw.
key.rookZone: The same pawn, but now the white king is close. It arrives in time, even letting the pawn queen, and mates together with the queen.
key.bishopDraw: Bishop pawn with the white king one step too far away: the black king hides in the corner, and capturing the pawn would leave it stalemated. A draw.
key.lolli: Lolli's study from 1763: the black king is on the side away from the corner. The queen holds the pawn, the white king comes closer and White mates.
key.trap: A trap for Black: only one escape saves the game, going straight to the corner. Any other square lets the queen and the white king close the net.
key.longSide: The black king is on the side away from the corner: there is no stalemate here, and a single well-chosen queen check wins.
key.vanWely: Van Wely against Leko, 1996: the bishop pawn reached the last square but one with the black king in the corner, and the white king was far away. The queen could not win.
key.fischer: The position the Petrosian–Fischer game of 1958 would have reached: a bishop pawn about to queen and the white king far away. Knowing the queen cannot win, they agreed a draw.
history: Queen against pawn almost always wins. But there are two exceptions every player should know, because they save games that looked lost: the edge pawn and the bishop pawn, when they reach the last square but one with their king beside them and the enemy king is far away. In both cases the defending king hides in the corner, and the queen, unless careful, can only stalemate it. Giambattista Lolli, an eighteenth-century Italian, published a study in 1763 showing when the stronger side's king still arrives in time. In 1958 Petrosian and Fischer agreed a draw because of this stalemate, and in 1996 Van Wely, with the queen, could not beat Leko's bishop pawn. Nearly everything comes down to one count: where the king of the side with the queen is.
practice: Now the exception, with or without a clock. A bishop pawn on the seventh, but your king is close. Keep the black king on the long side and bring your king into the zone.
